archetype.name: Improviser (refined)
archetype.definition: A third-year quarterback who still holds the ball and wins outside structure, scrambling for chunks, but who has paired that with the cleanest ball placement in the league over his first three starts.

report.headline: The accuracy leap looks real; now the offense needs him to push it downfield.
report.take:
Williams has always been a play-extender. He holds the ball, his time to throw sits at 3.26 seconds, and when the pocket breaks he runs for yardage rather than for safety. What has changed in 2026 is everything that happens when he actually lets go. Last year he completed 58.1% with a -3.5 CPOE and a bad-throw rate of 17.8%. Through three starts he is at 72.5% with an 8.76 CPOE, first among 45 qualifiers, and his bad-throw rate has fallen to 6.6%, second best charted. The improvement in bad throws is the number to trust most. Completion percentage can be inflated by easy throws, but a sharp drop in uncatchable balls usually reflects mechanics and decision-making.

The efficiency is spread across depths, and it is strongest beyond 10 air yards. His 25 throws of 10+ yards are worth 0.7 EPA each, and the intermediate band alone sits at 0.794. Kalif Raymond (0.739 EPA per target) and Rome Odunze (1.039) have been the ones cashing it. His 0.282 EPA per dropback ranks seventh. The legs add value in the form of scrambles: 11 of them, at 0.786 EPA each, producing six first downs. Designed runs subtract value, at -0.701 per play with more than half of them stuffed.

The box score hides two things. The first is the sacks. A 9% sack rate ranks 37th, and Atlanta got him four times. Even so, his pressure-to-sack rate of 20.8% is far from the 43.5% disaster of his rookie year and close to last season's 15.9%. That makes the sacks look more like the price of extending plays behind a line that let him be pressured 40.6% of the time against Minnesota than like a relapse. The second is that the throws have been getting shorter. His intended air yards were 10.4 in Week 1, then 3.9 and 3.6 in the next two games. Against Atlanta that produced a tidy 30-of-36 for 305 yards, but it is a narrower way to play than the one that carried Week 1.

The touchdown rate of 3.3% ranks 32nd. That is the clearest regression-upward candidate on the card for a quarterback who threw 27 touchdowns last year. He missed Weeks 3 through 5, so all of this rests on three games and 91 attempts. The direction is still encouraging: if the accuracy holds even partway and Ben Johnson lets him take more downfield shots, the box score should start catching up to the efficiency.

strengths.title: Ball placement transformed from last year
strengths.body: His CPOE leads all qualifiers, and his bad-throw rate has dropped by double digits from 2025. Uncatchable throws were his signature flaw for two seasons, so this is a real change in how he delivers the ball. CPOE will likely cool from 8.76. The bad-throw improvement is the part most likely to stick.

strengths.title: Damage beyond ten air yards
strengths.body: Only 25 of his attempts traveled 10+ yards, yet they produced more total EPA than his 66 shorter throws. The intermediate window has been especially productive, with Raymond and Odunze the main beneficiaries. The sample is small, but it argues for more of these throws, not fewer.

strengths.title: Scrambles that pay for themselves
strengths.body: He scrambles on nearly a tenth of his dropbacks, and those plays average 0.786 EPA with six first downs. That production is a big part of why the long time to throw is a trade worth making. His rushing has ranked seventh in each of his first two seasons, so this is part of who he is.

concerns.title: Sack rate near the bottom
concerns.body: A 9% sack rate ranks 37th of 45. It comes from holding the ball and being pressured, not from collapsing under pressure: his pressure-to-sack rate is a respectable 20.8% and close to last year's top-five mark. It is mostly the cost of his style, but four sacks in his last game shows how fast it can kill drives. A healthy Jonah Jackson at guard matters here.

concerns.title: Throws getting shorter
concerns.body: His intended air yards collapsed after Week 1, to 3.6 at Atlanta. In a run-leaning offense that already passes less than expected, a steady diet of short throws caps his touchdown and yardage ceiling. The team's own split data says the deeper throws are where his value lies.

concerns.title: Designed runs going nowhere
concerns.body: Called runs for him have been a drain, with 57.1% stuffed and negative EPA, including -7.8 rushing EPA against Atlanta. His running value is almost entirely in scrambles. The fix is a play-calling one, and it is not a flaw in his game.

trend.note: He opened with an 18.6-EPA blowout of Carolina and then managed -1 against Minnesota, the league's top defense, before missing three weeks. He came back with a short, efficient game at Atlanta, though the downfield element shrank across those three starts.

nextGame.headline: Patriots lose their every-down corner; the deep shot should open.
nextGame.body:
New England's defense is middle of the pack in EPA allowed, both overall and through the air. It has given up only 14 PPR points a game to quarterbacks, which ranks sixth, so the fantasy history is not inviting. Its weaknesses line up with Williams' best throws: the Patriots rank 24th in deep-pass EPA allowed, and their run defense is 23rd. Its sack rate sits 14th, a step down from the Minnesota front that swarmed him. The Bears are 3-point home favorites with a 50.5 total, which points to enough of a scoring environment for volume, though it comes on a four-day turnaround.

Availability tilts toward Chicago. Carlton Davis III, who plays 95% of New England's snaps at corner, is out, and two depth corners are out with him, so the Patriots will be stretched in the secondary. Their offense is also banged up: A.J. Brown and three offensive linemen are questionable and Romeo Doubs is on IR. That could cool the shootout, especially against a Bears defense with the league's second-best sack rate. On Williams' side, guard Jonah Jackson is questionable with a hip, and his status matters for a quarterback who holds the ball. Backup back Kyle Monangai is out, which funnels more work to D'Andre Swift, an efficient receiver for Williams so far.

keyMatchups.title: Intermediate and deep throws vs. thinned secondary
keyMatchups.body: Williams has been at his best on throws of 10+ yards, and New England is 24th in deep EPA allowed even before losing Davis. If the Bears call those throws, this is the spot to take them. The sample on both sides is thin, but the injuries reinforce the edge.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end lane is closed
keyMatchups.body: The Patriots have smothered opposing top tight ends, third-best in EPA per target allowed. Colston Loveland has been only modestly productive anyway. Expect the targets to tilt to the wideouts and Swift, whose role New England has defended poorly.

keyMatchups.title: Protection with Jackson questionable
keyMatchups.body: His 9% sack rate is the main thing that can derail an otherwise efficient day. New England's pass rush is only average, but missing a 94%-snap guard on a short week would make his long holds riskier.

nextGame.watch: Whether his intended air yards climb back toward Week 1 levels against a secondary missing Davis.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy gains should mostly hold. The bad-throw drop is too large to be pure noise, but a league-leading CPOE will drift down as the sample grows. The bigger move should come in the box score. A 3.3% touchdown rate is out of line with his efficiency and his 2025 production, so expect touchdowns to arrive more often even in a run-leaning offense. Sacks should ease toward his career pressure-to-sack skill without ever disappearing, given how long he holds the ball.

The ceiling depends on play-calling. If the offense keeps living near the line of scrimmage, he becomes an efficient 230-yard passer whose scrambles add a floor. If the intermediate and deep throws return, his early-season splits suggest top-ten quarterback production. Avoiding further missed time is its own variable after the Week 3-5 absence.
swingFactors: How often Johnson dials up 10+ yard throws
Pass protection and Jonah Jackson's health
Staying on the field after missing Weeks 3-5

confidence.note: Only three starts and 91 attempts, but the career data gives context for the sacks and the accuracy jump.
